```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H", out.extra = ""
)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
  library(kableExtra)
  library(patchwork)
})

source(file.path("..", "R", "03-fit-models.R"))

processed <- readRDS(file.path("..", "data", "processed", "marathon.rds"))
all_finishers <- processed$all_finishers
run <- processed$analysis

fits <- fit_marathon_models(run)
primary <- fits$primary
log_model <- fits$log_log

coefs <- coef(primary)
b0 <- coefs[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 <- coefs[["half_min"]]
fit_summary <- summary(primary)
diag <- model_diagnostics(primary)

slope_classical <- test_slope(primary, benchmark = 2)
slope_robust <- test_slope(primary, benchmark = 2, robust = TRUE)
log_slope <- test_slope(log_model, benchmark = 1)

n_analysis <- nrow(run)
n_finishers <- nrow(all_finishers)
n_dropped <- n_finishers - n_analysis

pct_positive <- 100 * mean(run$second_half_min > run$half_min)
median_ratio <- median(run$split_ratio)

# Minutes by which the doubling rule falls short of the fitted prediction at a
# given halfway split: (beta0 + beta1 * x) - 2x.
shortfall <- function(x) b0 + (b1 - 2) * x
median_split <- median(run$half_min)
shortfall_median <- shortfall(median_split)
split_at_15min <- (15 - b0) / (b1 - 2)
pct_over_15min <- 100 * mean(run$half_min > split_at_15min)

spread_raw <- residual_spread_by_bin(primary, run$half_min)
spread_log <- residual_spread_by_bin(log_model, log(run$half_min))
spread_ratio_raw <- max(spread_raw$resid_sd) / min(spread_raw$resid_sd)
spread_ratio_log <- max(spread_log$resid_sd) / min(spread_log$resid_sd)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))
theme_update(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
)

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
hms <- function(minutes) {
  total <- round(minutes * 60)
  sprintf("%d:%02d:%02d", total %/% 3600, (total %% 3600) %/% 60, total %% 60)
}
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Runners and spectators routinely project a marathon finishing time by doubling
the time on the clock at halfway, but how far that rule is off, and for which
runners, is rarely quantified for a whole field. Using official results for
`r fmt(n_analysis, 0)` finishers of the
2023 Boston Marathon, distributed through the SCORE Network Sports Data
Repository [@fay2023boston], I fit a simple linear regression of net finishing
time on half-marathon split time. Each additional minute at halfway is
associated with `r fmt(b1, 3)` additional minutes at the finish (95% confidence
interval `r fmt(slope_classical$conf_low, 3)` to
`r fmt(slope_classical$conf_high, 3)`), which is reliably more than the two
minutes that even pacing would imply, and the halfway split predicts finishing
time with a residual standard deviation of about
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 1)` minutes. Because the gap widens as the halfway
split lengthens, slower runners lose proportionally more time over the second
half than faster runners do, and the familiar "double your halfway time" rule
understates the finish for nearly nine runners in ten. A more accurate rule for
this field is to double the halfway split and add roughly a further fifth of
it.

# Introduction

The half-marathon timing mat is the most visible checkpoint in a marathon. It
is where runners take stock of their race, where spectators guess when their
friend will appear, and where broadcast commentators project a winning time.
The projection almost always used is simple doubling: a runner passing halfway
in 1 hour 45 minutes is said to be "on pace" for 3 hours 30 minutes. That rule
is exactly right only if a runner covers the second half in the same time as
the first, and decades of race results suggest that most runners do not
[@march2011age; @santoslozano2014influence]. What is less often quantified, in a
form a runner can use at the mat, is by how much the rule errs, and whether it
errs equally for a 2:30 runner and a 5:00 runner.

Slowing over the second half of a marathon, known as positive splitting, has a
well-documented physiological basis: muscle glycogen depletion, rising core
temperature, and accumulated muscle damage all make the closing miles more
costly than the opening ones. The extent of the slowdown varies systematically
across runners. Slower and less experienced runners fade more than faster ones
[@march2011age], men fade more than women on average [@deaner2015men], warm
conditions amplify the effect, particularly for slower finishers
[@ely2008effect], and a sizeable minority of recreational runners experience a
pronounced late-race collapse [@smyth2021how]. Much of this work summarizes
pacing by comparing group averages, dividing fields into ability bands or
sex groups and reporting mean second-half slowdown within each band.

Comparing group means answers a descriptive question but not a predictive one.
A runner at the mat does not want to know the average slowdown of their
ability band; they want a single equation that converts their own split into an
expected finishing time, together with an honest statement of how far off that
estimate is likely to be. Simple linear regression supplies exactly that, and
it has an additional advantage here: the even-pacing rule corresponds to a
specific numerical value of the slope, namely two minutes of finishing time per
minute of halfway split. The usual regression null hypothesis of a zero slope
is uninformative in this setting, because finishing time must increase with the
halfway split. Testing the fitted slope against two, rather than against zero,
turns a routine regression into a direct test of whether a mass-participation
field paces evenly.

This paper therefore asks two linked questions of the full finishing field of
the 2023 Boston Marathon: how accurately does a runner's half-marathon split
predict their net finishing time, and does the fitted relationship depart from
the two minutes per minute that even pacing implies? The estimated slope is
`r fmt(b1, 3)` rather than 2, a difference
that is far larger than its standard error, so each extra minute taken to reach
halfway is associated with about `r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` extra minutes over the
second half instead of the one minute even pacing would require. The halfway
split explains almost all of the variation in finishing time, but the spread
that remains is practically wide: a prediction for an individual runner carries
an uncertainty of roughly `r fmt(2 * fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes in either
direction. The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
@sec-data describes the data set, its variables, and its limitations.
@sec-methods sets out the regression model, the assumptions behind it,
and the checks used to validate it. @sec-results reports the fitted
model and its practical implications, and @sec-discussion summarizes
the findings, the weaknesses of the study, and ways it could be extended.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Source and observational units

The data are the official results of the 2023 Boston Marathon, run on April 17,
2023. The file was compiled by @fay2023boston from results published by the
Boston Athletic Association [@baa2023results] and is distributed through the
SCORE Network Sports Data Repository. Each row is one runner who finished the
race, so the observational unit is a single finisher, and the data set covers
the complete finishing field of `r fmt(n_finishers, 0)` runners rather than a
sample from it. Runners who started but did not finish never appear in the
results, a point I return to below.

The times are not survey responses or hand-recorded observations: each runner
carries a timing chip that is detected by mats laid across the course, and the
organizer publishes the resulting table after the race. That collection process
shapes what the data can and cannot say. Times are recorded for every runner
who crosses a mat, so there is no sampling variability in the usual sense and
no non-response; the population of finishers is observed in full. What the
process cannot record is anything happening between mats, so a runner who
stopped for ten minutes at 30 km and one who slowed evenly throughout appear
identical if their halfway and finishing times agree. Entry to the race is also
selective. Most runners qualify by posting a time standard at an earlier
marathon, and the rest enter through charity programs, so the field is not a
random draw from marathon runners in general.

## Variables

The file contains 15 columns recording each finisher's identity, age group,
sex, finishing places, and times. Five are used here, and two further variables
are derived from them.

The response variable is **net finishing time**, the elapsed time from the
moment a runner crosses the starting mat to the moment they cross the finishing
mat, recorded by a timing chip and converted here from seconds to minutes.
Boston starts runners in waves and corrals, so the starting gun and a given
runner's actual start can differ considerably: across all finishers the gun
time exceeds the net time by a median of
`r fmt(median(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes
and by as much as
`r fmt(max(all_finishers$gun_min - all_finishers$finish_min), 1)` minutes. Net
time measures the runner's own race and is the appropriate response for a
question about pacing; gun time would mix in corral assignment, which reflects
qualifying time rather than what happened on the day.

The explanatory variable is the **half-marathon split**, the net elapsed time
recorded at the halfway timing mat, also converted to minutes. From these two I
derive **second-half time**, the difference between the finishing time and the
split, and the **split ratio**, the second-half time divided by the split. A
ratio above one means the runner covered the second half more slowly than the
first. **Sex** is recorded in the source file as `M` or `W`, and
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$sex == "Women"), 1)`% of the analyzed field is recorded as
women. **Age group** is recorded as one of ten bands rather than an exact age,
running from 18--39 through 80+; the largest band is 18--39, holding
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$age_group == "18-39"), 1)`% of finishers, so
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$age_group != "18-39"), 1)`% of this field are masters
runners aged 40 or over. Because age arrives banded, it could not serve as a
continuous predictor without assigning an arbitrary value to each band. Both
variables are used for description only and are not part of the fitted model.

Both times come from chip timing, which is accurate to about one second. That
error is negligible next to a standard deviation of
`r fmt(sd(run$half_min), 1)` minutes in the split, so measurement error in
either variable can be ignored. One structural feature of the variables does
matter and is addressed in @sec-methods: the finishing time contains
the halfway split, because a marathon is the sum of its two halves.

## Missing data and field characteristics

In all, `r n_dropped` finishers (`r fmt(100 * n_dropped / n_finishers, 2)`% of
the field) have no recorded half-marathon split, most likely because of a missed
chip read at the mat. Because the split is the explanatory variable, these
runners cannot enter the model and are dropped, leaving `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)`
runners. Their exclusion is unlikely to distort the results: their mean
finishing time,
`r fmt(mean(all_finishers$finish_min[is.na(all_finishers$half_min)]), 1)`
minutes, is close to the `r fmt(mean(run$finish_min), 1)` minutes of the
runners retained, and they are spread across sexes and age groups in much the
same proportions as the rest of the field. No other variable used here has
missing values, and no runner appears twice.

@tbl-summary summarizes the analysis variables. The field is wide
ranging: halfway splits run from `r hms(min(run$half_min))` to
`r hms(max(run$half_min))` and finishing times from `r hms(min(run$finish_min))`
to `r hms(max(run$finish_min))`. The median split ratio of
`r fmt(median_ratio, 3)` says that a typical finisher ran the second half about
`r fmt(100 * (median_ratio - 1), 1)`% slower than the first.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics for the four analysis variables, across all 26,526 finishers of the 2023 Boston Marathon who have a recorded half-marathon split. Times are in minutes; the split ratio is second-half time divided by half-marathon split and is unitless. All three time variables are right skewed, with means above their medians and maxima far above the third quartile, which is why the field's slowest runners dominate the upper tail. The split ratio has a median of 1.058, so the typical finisher took about 6 percent longer over the second half than the first, and its minimum below 1 shows that a minority ran the second half faster."
describe_variable <- function(values, label, digits) {
  quartiles <- quantile(values, c(0.25, 0.75))
  data.frame(
    Variable = label,
    Mean = mean(values),
    SD = stats::sd(values),
    Min = min(values),
    Q1 = quartiles[[1]],
    Median = median(values),
    Q3 = quartiles[[2]],
    Max = max(values)
  ) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = digits)))
}

summary_table <- bind_rows(
  describe_variable(run$half_min, "Half-marathon split (min)", 1),
  describe_variable(run$finish_min, "Net finishing time (min)", 1),
  describe_variable(run$second_half_min, "Second-half time (min)", 1),
  describe_variable(run$split_ratio, "Split ratio (unitless)", 3)
)

kable(
  summary_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", rep("r", 7))
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 8)
```

Pacing was similar for women and men even though their finishing times were
not. Median finishing time was `r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Women"]))`
for the `r fmt(sum(run$sex == "Women"), 0)` women and
`r hms(median(run$finish_min[run$sex == "Men"]))` for the
`r fmt(sum(run$sex == "Men"), 0)` men, yet the median split ratio was
`r fmt(median(run$split_ratio), 3)` in both groups, and the share running a
slower second half was
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$second_half_min[run$sex == "Women"] > run$half_min[run$sex == "Women"]), 1)`%
and
`r fmt(100 * mean(run$second_half_min[run$sex == "Men"] > run$half_min[run$sex == "Men"]), 1)`%
respectively. Sex is therefore not a strong candidate for explaining the
pacing pattern in this field, which supports treating the halfway split as the
single explanatory variable in @sec-methods.

Two features of the field shape how far the results travel. First, Boston is
not an open race: most entrants qualify by running a time standard at an
earlier marathon, and the remainder enter through charity programs. The field
is therefore faster and more experienced than a typical city marathon, and if
experience protects against fading, the slowdown measured here is likely to be
milder than it would be in an open field. Second, every runner in these data
raced the same course on the same day, and ambient temperature is known to
affect how much runners slow, with slower runners most affected
[@ely2008effect]. Because conditions do not vary within the data set, their
effect cannot be separated from pacing behavior; whatever the weather on the
day contributed is absorbed into the estimated relationship.

@fig-distributions shows the distributions of the two modeled
variables and of the split ratio. Both time distributions are right skewed,
with a long tail of slower finishers. The split ratio is centered a little above
one and has a pronounced right tail: `r fmt(pct_positive, 1)`% of finishers ran
a slower second half, and a small group took more than twice as long over the
second half as the first.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the two modeled variables and of the split ratio for 26,526 finishers. Half-marathon split (left) and net finishing time (center) are both right skewed. The split ratio (right, second-half time divided by half-marathon time) is centered just above the dashed even-pacing line at 1.0, showing that a slower second half was the norm: 89.0% of finishers ran a positive split. The horizontal axis of the right panel is restricted to 0.8--1.6 for legibility, which hides 0.15% of runners whose pacing was more extreme still; the most uneven runner took more than twice as long over the second half as over the first."
p1 <- ggplot(run, aes(half_min)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (min)", y = "Runners")

p2 <- ggplot(run, aes(finish_min)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  labs(x = "Net finishing time (min)", y = "Runners")

p3 <- ggplot(run, aes(split_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = "Split ratio (2nd half / 1st half)", y = "Runners")

p1 + p2 + p3
```

## Additional and alternative data

The published results contain richer pacing information than this file
includes: the Boston Athletic Association records splits at 5 km intervals as
well as at halfway, which would allow the shape of the slowdown to be traced
rather than summarized by a single second-half figure. Results for other
editions of the race are published in the same format, and other large
marathons publish comparable files, so the analysis could be repeated across
years and courses. Hourly weather observations for the course are available
from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and could be matched
to each runner's time on the course, which would help separate heat effects
from pacing behavior. Qualifying times, which the results do not include,
would give a measure of each runner's recent fitness and so distinguish a
runner who paced badly from one who was simply having a poor day. None of these
sources is needed for the question asked here, but each would support the
extensions discussed in @sec-discussion.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## The model

Let $Y_i$ denote the net finishing time in minutes of runner $i$ and let $x_i$
denote that runner's half-marathon split in minutes, for
$i = 1, \dots, n$ with $n = `r fmt(n_analysis, 0)`$. The simple linear
regression model is

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
  \varepsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).$$

Here $\beta_0$ is the intercept, the expected finishing time for a runner with
a halfway split of zero minutes; $\beta_1$ is the slope, the expected increase
in finishing time associated with a one-minute increase in the halfway split;
$\varepsilon_i$ is the error for runner $i$, the amount by which that runner's
actual finishing time departs from the mean for runners with the same split;
and $\sigma^2$ is the variance of those errors, assumed the same for every
runner. The notation $\stackrel{iid}{\sim}$ means the errors are independent of
one another and drawn from the same normal distribution.

The parameters are estimated by ordinary least squares, which chooses the
values $\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$ minimizing the sum of squared vertical
distances between the observed finishing times and the fitted line,
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2$. Writing $\bar{x}$ and
$\bar{Y}$ for the sample means, the minimizing values are

$$\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}
                     {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2},
  \qquad
  \hat\beta_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}.$$

The residual for runner $i$ is $e_i = Y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i$, and
the residual standard deviation
$\hat\sigma = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 / (n - 2)}$ estimates $\sigma$. Two
degrees of freedom are subtracted because the intercept and slope have been
estimated from the same data. Reporting $\hat\sigma$ in minutes makes it
directly readable as the precision of a prediction. The standard error of the
slope,

$$SE(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}},$$

shows why the estimate here is so precise: the denominator grows with both the
number of runners and the spread of their halfway splits, and this field is
large and widely spread on both counts. Under the assumptions listed in
@sec-assumptions, least squares is unbiased for $\beta_0$ and
$\beta_1$ and has the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators.

For an individual runner with halfway split $x_0$, the model predicts
$\hat{Y}_0 = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0$, and a 95% prediction interval for
that runner's actual finishing time is

$$\hat{Y}_0 \pm t_{0.975,\,n-2}\;\hat\sigma
  \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0 - \bar{x})^2}
                               {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}.$$

The leading 1 under the square root is the individual runner's own deviation
from the line, which is why a prediction interval for one runner is far wider
than a confidence interval for the average runner at the same split, and why it
barely narrows as the sample grows.

A single explanatory variable is appropriate because the question is itself a
one-variable question: it asks what a runner can infer at the halfway mat, when
the split is the only new information available. Sex, age, and weather all
influence finishing time, but adding them would answer a different question and
would produce an equation a runner could not evaluate from the clock.

## The even-pacing benchmark

If every runner covered the two halves of the course in equal times, then
$Y_i = 2x_i$ exactly, which corresponds to $\beta_0 = 0$ and $\beta_1 = 2$. The
slope therefore has a meaningful benchmark value, and the hypotheses of
interest are

$$H_0: \beta_1 = 2 \qquad \text{versus} \qquad H_1: \beta_1 \neq 2,$$

tested with the statistic $t = (\hat\beta_1 - 2) / SE(\hat\beta_1)$ compared to
a $t$ distribution with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom. A slope above two means
that a one-minute increase in the halfway split is associated with more than
one extra minute in the second half, so that runners who reach halfway later
also give up proportionally more time afterwards. The conventional test of
$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is reported by software automatically but carries no
information here, since finishing time cannot fail to increase with the halfway
split.

The same question can be posed by regressing second-half time on the halfway
split. Because second-half time is $Y_i - x_i$, that model has slope
$\beta_1 - 1$ and identical standard errors, so it tests the even-pacing
benchmark of one with exactly the same $t$ statistic. The choice between the
two framings is presentational, and I use finishing time as the response
because it is the quantity a runner wants to predict.

One consequence of this structure deserves emphasis. The response contains the
explanatory variable by construction, since a finishing time is the halfway
split plus the second-half time. A large $R^2$ is therefore guaranteed and
should not be read as evidence that pacing is well understood; it mostly
reflects the arithmetic. The informative quantities are the distance of the
slope from two, which is not mechanical, and the residual standard deviation,
which measures how precisely the second half can be anticipated.

## Assumptions and diagnostics {#sec-assumptions}

Four assumptions support the model, and I checked each.

**Linearity.** The mean finishing time is assumed to change at a constant rate
across the range of halfway splits. A scatterplot with the fitted line and a
plot of residuals against fitted values were used to look for curvature.

**Independence.** Errors are assumed unrelated across runners. This is the
weakest assumption in the analysis: runners race in packs, follow pacing
groups, and share the same weather and course conditions, so two runners near
each other are likely to fade together. Clustering of this kind leaves the
slope estimate unbiased but can make standard errors too small. With a
confidence interval already narrow enough that the conclusion does not turn on
its width, the practical risk is limited, but the assumption cannot be verified
from the results file alone.

**Constant variance.** Residual spread should not change with the fitted value.
It plainly does here, so this assumption fails; @sec-selection sets out how I
handle it.

**Normality.** The errors are assumed normally distributed. A normal
quantile-quantile plot shows heavy tails, and the residuals are right skewed.
For inference about $\beta_1$ this matters little, because with tens of
thousands of observations the sampling distribution of the slope is
approximately normal regardless. It matters more for prediction intervals for
an individual runner, which rely on the shape of the error distribution rather
than on large-sample behavior, so those intervals are reported as
approximations.

Influence was assessed with Cook's distance, which measures how much the fitted
line would move if a single runner were removed. The largest value in the data
is `r fmt(diag$max_cooks, 3)`, far below the conventional threshold of one, so
no individual result drives the fit. Unusual pacing patterns, including runners
who walked large parts of the first half and those who collapsed in the second,
were deliberately retained: they are genuine race outcomes rather than
recording errors, and removing them would bias the estimated slowdown toward
zero.

## Model selection and validation {#sec-selection}

Two specifications were considered: the model above, fitted on the original
minute scale, and the same regression with both variables on the natural log
scale. I selected the original scale as the primary model on interpretability
grounds. The even-pacing benchmark is exactly 2 on that scale, so the
hypothesis test answers the research question directly, and the slope and
residual standard deviation are both in minutes, which is the unit a runner
reasons in. The log-log fit is retained not as a rival but as a check: if it
reversed the conclusion, the primary model could not be trusted. Choosing
between them on fit alone would be the wrong criterion, because the two have
different response variables and their $R^2$ values are not comparable.

That choice leaves the constant-variance failure to deal with. Because residual
spread grows with the halfway split, the least squares estimates remain
unbiased but the usual standard errors are not trustworthy. I addressed this in
two ways, which together form the validation step for the model.

First, I recomputed the standard error of the slope using a
heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC1) estimator [@zeileis2004sandwich], which
does not assume constant variance. Second, I refitted the model with both
variables on the natural log scale,

$$\log(Y_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \log(x_i) + \eta_i,$$

where $\gamma_1$ is the elasticity of finishing time with respect to the
halfway split: the approximate percentage change in finishing time associated
with a 1% increase in the split. Even pacing implies
$\log(Y_i) = \log 2 + \log(x_i)$, so the benchmark for $\gamma_1$ is one rather
than two, and a value above one again means that slower runners fade
proportionally more. Taking logarithms compresses the long right tail of both
variables and is the standard remedy when spread grows with level. If the
conclusion about pacing survives both changes, it does not depend on the
assumption that failed. Formal evidence for non-constant variance is provided
by the Breusch--Pagan test [@breusch1979simple; @zeileis2002lmtest].

## Possible extensions to the model

Three extensions would change the analysis in predictable ways. Adding sex and
age group as further explanatory variables, with interactions against the
halfway split, would turn the model into a multiple regression and would let the
slope differ across groups; since men and women in this field slowed by almost
the same proportion (@tbl-summary), this is likely to sharpen
the intercept more than the slope, and it would cost the equation its usability
at the mat. Allowing curvature, through a quadratic term or a spline in the
split, would relax the constant-rate assumption; the residual plot shows little
curvature, so the fitted values would move only slightly, but any extrapolation
beyond the observed range would become less stable. Weighted least squares or
quantile regression would model the growing spread directly rather than
correcting for it after the fact; the slope estimate would change little,
because the robust and log-log refits already leave it intact, but the
prediction intervals would widen for slower runners and narrow for faster ones,
which is where the present intervals are least accurate. None of these
extensions is required to answer the question posed here, and each is set out
more fully in @sec-discussion.

## Software

All work was carried out in R version
`r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")` [@rcore2024]. Data
handling used **dplyr** [@wickham2023dplyr] and **readr**
[@wickham2024readr]; figures were produced with **ggplot2**
[@wickham2016ggplot2] and assembled with **patchwork**
[@pedersen2024patchwork]; robust standard errors and the Breusch--Pagan test
came from **sandwich** [@zeileis2020sandwich; @zeileis2004sandwich] and
**lmtest** [@zeileis2002lmtest]; and the report was generated with **knitr**
[@xie2023knitr], **rmarkdown** [@xie2018rmarkdown], **bookdown**
[@xie2016bookdown], and **kableExtra** [@zhu2024kableextra]. Models were fitted
with the `lm` function in R's built-in **stats** package.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The fitted model

The fitted regression line is

$$\widehat{\text{finish}} = `r fmt(b0, 2)` + `r fmt(b1, 3)` \times
  \text{half-marathon split},$$

with both times in minutes. @tbl-coefs reports the estimates.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Ordinary least squares estimates for the regression of net finishing time (minutes) on half-marathon split (minutes), fitted to 26,526 finishers of the 2023 Boston Marathon. Confidence intervals are 95% intervals based on constant-variance standard errors. The slope of 2.218 exceeds the value of 2 implied by even pacing, and the interval for the slope excludes 2 by a wide margin."
coef_table <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Intercept", "Half-marathon split"),
  Estimate = c(b0, b1),
  `Std. error` = c(fit_summary$coefficients[1, 2], fit_summary$coefficients[2, 2]),
  `CI low` = confint(primary)[, 1],
  `CI high` = confint(primary)[, 2],
  check.names = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Estimate, `CI low`, `CI high`), ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = 3)),
    `Std. error` = formatC(`Std. error`, format = "g", digits = 3)
  )

kable(
  coef_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

The slope of `r fmt(b1, 3)` is the central result. A runner who reaches halfway
one minute later than another runner is expected to finish
`r fmt(b1, 2)` minutes later, not the two minutes that equal halves would
imply. Rearranged, each extra minute taken to reach halfway is associated with
`r fmt(b1 - 1, 2)` extra minutes over the second half. Comparing the estimate
with the even-pacing benchmark gives
$t = `r fmt(slope_classical$t_statistic, 1)`$ on
`r fmt(slope_classical$df, 0)` degrees of freedom, with a $p$-value below
0.001, so a field that paces evenly on average is not consistent with these
results. The 95% confidence interval for the slope,
`r fmt(slope_classical$conf_low, 3)` to
`r fmt(slope_classical$conf_high, 3)`, lies entirely above two.

The intercept of `r fmt(b0, 2)` minutes has no physical meaning on its own: a
halfway split of zero minutes is impossible, and the observed splits range from
`r fmt(min(run$half_min), 1)` to `r fmt(max(run$half_min), 1)` minutes, so a
split of zero is far outside the data. Its only role is to place the line
correctly over the range of splits that runners actually record. Its negative value is what allows a line with
a slope steeper than two to pass through the middle of a field in which typical
finishing times are close to twice the halfway split.

The model accounts for `r fmt(100 * fit_summary$r.squared, 1)`% of the variation
in finishing times, and the correlation between the two times is
`r fmt(cor(run$half_min, run$finish_min), 3)`. As explained in
@sec-methods, these figures are inflated by the fact that finishing time
contains the halfway split, and they should not be read as a measure of how
well pacing is understood. The residual standard deviation of
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 2)` minutes is the more useful summary of fit: the
typical runner finishes within about `r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes of
the prediction made from their halfway split.

@fig-scatter shows the data with the fitted line and the
even-pacing line $y = 2x$ for comparison. The fitted line sits above the
even-pacing line across the whole range and pulls further above it as splits
lengthen, which is the visual signature of a slope greater than two.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-cap: "Net finishing time against half-marathon split for 26,526 finishers of the 2023 Boston Marathon, with each point one runner (plotted with transparency so that darker regions indicate more runners). The solid line is the fitted regression, finish = -14.53 + 2.218 x split; the dashed line is the even-pacing reference finish = 2 x split. The fitted line lies above the reference line throughout and diverges from it as splits lengthen, showing that runners who reach halfway later lose proportionally more time over the second half. Points above the dashed line are runners who slowed in the second half."
ggplot(run, aes(half_min, finish_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.35, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = 2, intercept = 0, linetype = "Even pacing (y = 2x)"),
    colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    aes(slope = b1, intercept = b0, linetype = "Fitted regression"),
    colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Even pacing (y = 2x)" = "dashed", "Fitted regression" = "solid"),
    name = NULL,
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      colour = c("#B2182B", "#2166AC"), linewidth = 0.7
    ))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Half-marathon split (minutes)", y = "Net finishing time (minutes)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## What the model means for a runner

@tbl-predictions converts the fitted line into the projections a
runner might make at the mat. For each halfway split it gives the finishing
time the doubling rule predicts, the finishing time the model predicts, and an
approximate 95% prediction interval for an individual runner.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Finishing times projected from five halfway splits, comparing the doubling rule with the fitted regression. The final column gives the number of minutes by which doubling understates the model prediction; it grows with the halfway split, from about 5 minutes for a 1:30 split to about 18 minutes for a 2:30 split. Prediction intervals are approximate because the residuals are heavy tailed, and they are wide -- roughly 37 minutes across -- which shows that the halfway split pins down the average finishing time far more precisely than any individual runner's."
pred_points <- data.frame(half_min = c(90, 105, 120, 135, 150))
pred_fit <- predict(primary, newdata = pred_points, interval = "prediction")

pred_table <- data.frame(
  `Halfway split` = vapply(pred_points$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  `Doubling rule` = vapply(2 * pred_points$half_min, hms, character(1)),
  `Model prediction` = vapply(pred_fit[, "fit"], hms, character(1)),
  `95% prediction interval` = paste0(
    vapply(pred_fit[, "lwr"], hms, character(1)), " to ",
    vapply(pred_fit[, "upr"], hms, character(1))
  ),
  `Shortfall of doubling` = paste0(
    formatC(pred_fit[, "fit"] - 2 * pred_points$half_min, format = "f", digits = 1),
    " min"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  pred_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 8)
```

The shortfall of the doubling rule grows across the table, from about
`r fmt(shortfall(90), 0)` minutes for a runner passing halfway in 1:30 to about
`r fmt(shortfall(150), 0)` minutes for a runner passing in 2:30. This is the
practical form of the result: the faster the runner, the better the doubling
rule works. For the median finisher, who reached halfway in
`r hms(median_split)`, doubling understates the finish by about
`r fmt(shortfall_median, 0)` minutes, and the shortfall reaches a quarter of an
hour only for the slowest `r fmt(pct_over_15min, 0)`% of the field. The
prediction intervals,
however, are wide: about `r fmt(diff(pred_fit[1, c("lwr", "upr")]), 0)` minutes
from bottom to top. The regression describes the average behavior of the field
accurately while leaving a great deal of individual variation unexplained,
which is what one would expect given that the second half of a marathon depends
on training, fueling, heat tolerance, and luck that the halfway clock cannot
observe.

The descriptive pacing figures agree with the model: a slower second half was
run by `r fmt(pct_positive, 1)`% of finishers, and the median runner's second
half was `r fmt(100 * (median_ratio - 1), 1)`% slower than their first.

## Model checking

@fig-diagnostics presents the diagnostics described in
@sec-methods. The residual plot is roughly flat, so the straight-line form is
adequate, but the band of residuals widens markedly from left to right. The
residual standard deviation rises from
`r fmt(min(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)` minutes among the fastest tenth of the
field to `r fmt(max(spread_raw$resid_sd), 1)` minutes among the slowest, a
`r fmt(spread_ratio_raw, 1)`-fold increase, and the Breusch--Pagan test rejects
constant variance decisively ($BP = `r fmt(diag$bp_test$statistic, 1)`$ on
`r diag$bp_test$parameter` degree of freedom, $p < 0.001$). The quantile-quantile plot shows
approximate normality through the center with heavy tails at both ends, the
right tail reflecting runners who faded badly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Regression diagnostics for the fitted model. Top left: residuals against fitted values, flat on average (so a straight line is adequate) but fanning out as fitted times increase. Top right: normal quantile-quantile plot of standardized residuals, close to the reference line through the center but with heavy tails at both ends. Bottom: residual standard deviation within tenths of the half-marathon split, expressed relative to the fastest decile so that the two fits can be compared on one scale. On the original scale the spread grows 2.4-fold across the field, which is why the constant-variance assumption fails; on the log-log scale it grows only 1.4-fold, which is why that fit is used as a sensitivity check."
aug <- diag$augmented

d1 <- ggplot(aug, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Fitted finishing time (min)", y = "Residual (min)",
       title = "Residuals vs fitted")

qq <- data.frame(sample = aug$std_resid)
d2 <- ggplot(qq, aes(sample = sample)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.06, size = 0.3, colour = "grey25") +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Standardized residual",
       title = "Normal Q-Q")

spread_compare <- bind_rows(
  spread_raw %>%
    transmute(split = mean_predictor,
              relative_sd = resid_sd / resid_sd[1],
              Model = "Original scale"),
  spread_log %>%
    transmute(split = exp(mean_predictor),
              relative_sd = resid_sd / resid_sd[1],
              Model = "Log-log scale")
)

d3 <- ggplot(spread_compare, aes(split, relative_sd, colour = Model, shape = Model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Original scale" = "#2166AC", "Log-log scale" = "#B2182B")) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean half-marathon split within decile (minutes)",
    y = "Residual SD relative\nto fastest decile",
    title = "Growth in residual spread across the field",
    colour = NULL, shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

(d1 + d2) / d3
```

@tbl-sensitivity shows that the conclusion is unaffected by either
remedy. Robust standard errors roughly `r fmt(slope_robust$std_error / slope_classical$std_error, 1)`
times the constant-variance ones still place the slope far above two
($t = `r fmt(slope_robust$t_statistic, 1)`$). On the log-log scale the
elasticity is `r fmt(coef(log_model)[[2]], 3)`, again above the even-pacing
benchmark of one ($t = `r fmt(log_slope$t_statistic, 1)`$), and the residual
spread across deciles rises by a factor of only
`r fmt(spread_ratio_log, 1)` rather than `r fmt(spread_ratio_raw, 1)`, so the
transformation does most of the work of stabilizing the variance. Both versions
of the model say the same thing: runners who reach halfway later give up
proportionally more time in the second half.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the pacing conclusion to the failure of the constant-variance assumption. Each row tests the fitted slope against the value implied by even pacing (2 on the original scale, 1 on the log-log scale). Robust standard errors widen the interval slightly and the log-log model changes the scale entirely, but in all three versions the slope sits far above its even-pacing benchmark, so the conclusion does not depend on the assumption that failed."
sens_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Original scale, constant-variance SE",
    "Original scale, robust (HC1) SE",
    "Log-log scale, constant-variance SE"
  ),
  Slope = formatC(c(b1, b1, coef(log_model)[[2]]), format = "f", digits = 3),
  `Std. error` = formatC(
    c(slope_classical$std_error, slope_robust$std_error, log_slope$std_error),
    format = "f", digits = 4
  ),
  Benchmark = c("2", "2", "1"),
  `t statistic` = formatC(
    c(slope_classical$t_statistic, slope_robust$t_statistic, log_slope$t_statistic),
    format = "f", digits = 1
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(
  sens_table, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Across the full finishing field of the 2023 Boston Marathon, finishing time
rises by `r fmt(b1, 2)` minutes for each additional minute of half-marathon
split, rather than the two minutes that even pacing implies. The doubling rule
used at the halfway mat is therefore biased, and predictably so: it is nearly
right for the fastest runners, understates the finish by about
`r fmt(shortfall_median, 0)` minutes for the median finisher, and is optimistic
by a quarter of an hour or more for the slowest
`r fmt(pct_over_15min, 0)`% of the field. Replacing it with the fitted
line, or with the rough mental version of doubling the split and adding a
further fifth of it, removes that bias. The wide prediction intervals are as
important as the slope: the halfway split fixes the field's average behavior
tightly but leaves an individual runner's finish uncertain by roughly
`r fmt(fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes on average and by about
`r fmt(2 * fit_summary$sigma, 0)` minutes either side at the 95% level, so the
projection should be treated as a central estimate rather than a forecast. That slower runners fade
more is consistent with previous findings from other marathons
[@march2011age; @santoslozano2014influence], and this analysis adds a single
directly usable equation for a complete mass-participation field.

Several weaknesses qualify these conclusions. The data describe finishers only.
Runners who started and dropped out are absent from the results, and they are
disproportionately the runners whose second half went worst, so the true
average slowdown in the starting field is steeper than the estimate here: the
result is a lower bound on fading. The analysis covers one race on one day, and
Boston's qualifying standards make its field faster and more experienced than an
open marathon, so the numerical slope should not be transferred to a different
race without refitting. Conditions on the day are absorbed into the estimate
and cannot be separated from it. The constant-variance assumption fails outright and
the residuals are heavy tailed; robust standard errors and a log-log refit leave
the conclusion intact, but the prediction intervals remain approximate and are
probably too narrow for the slowest runners and too wide for the fastest.
Runners influence each other's pacing, which the independence assumption
ignores. Finally, the model is descriptive, not causal: it does not show that
starting faster causes a better finish, since runners who reach halfway quickly
are fitter, and fitness rather than pace choice explains much of the
association.

The natural extensions follow from those limitations. Adding sex, age group,
and their interactions with the halfway split would test whether the slowdown
differs across runners in the way earlier work reports [@deaner2015men], at the
cost of an equation a runner could no longer evaluate from the clock alone.
Fitting the same model to several editions of the race, with a weather variable
for each day, would separate heat effects from pacing behavior and would show
whether the slope is a stable property of the field [@ely2008effect]. The 5 km
splits published by the organizers would allow the slowdown to be traced
through the race rather than summarized once, which is the natural way to study
late-race collapse [@smyth2021how]. Quantile regression would model the spread
directly instead of treating it as a nuisance, and would give runners
prediction limits that widen appropriately with their split. Each of these
would refine the estimate; none is likely to overturn the central finding, which
is that a marathon field does not pace evenly, and that the shortfall of the
doubling rule grows with the time on the clock at halfway.
